blocks.text: **The problem.** Group the elements of a matrix by **diagonal**, where each diagonal runs from bottom-left to top-right, and return the groups in order starting from the top-left corner.

blocks.alt: A 3 by 3 matrix coloured by diagonal. The five diagonals are [1], [2, 4], [3, 5, 7], [6, 8] and [9]. Every cell on a diagonal has the same row plus column.

blocks.text: Example
Understanding the problem

The shape of each diagonal changes: they grow longer toward the middle and shorter again after it. Trying to compute the start and end cell of each diagonal gets messy fast, especially for non-square matrices.
The key insight: r + c is constant along a diagonal

The whole problem collapses once you notice this: **every cell on the same diagonal has the same value of `r + c`**. Moving down-left increases `r` by one and decreases `c` by one, so the sum never changes.
Cells with sum 0 form the first diagonal, sum 1 the second, and so on. A matrix with R rows and C columns has **R + C − 1** diagonals.
The approach: buckets keyed by r + c
No clever traversal order is needed. Sweep the grid normally, row by row, and drop each value into the bucket numbered `r + c`.
Dry run it yourself
Each value highlights its diagonal and lands at the end of its bucket. Try a non-square matrix like `1 2 3 4; 5 6 7 8`.
Code
Ordering within a diagonal

A row-by-row sweep visits `(0, 2)` before `(1, 1)` before `(2, 0)`, so each bucket fills from **top-right to bottom-left**. If you need the opposite direction, sweep the rows in reverse, or reverse each bucket afterwards.
The popular **zigzag** variant ("Diagonal Traverse") alternates direction on each diagonal. It's this same solution plus one line: reverse the even-numbered buckets, then flatten them into one list.

blocks.code:
const zigzag = diagonalGroups(matrix)
  .flatMap((group, d) => (d % 2 === 0 ? group.reverse() : group));

blocks.text: Complexity

blocks.alt: Diagonal traversal: O(rows × cols) time and O(rows × cols) space for the buckets.

blocks.text: One ordinary sweep: **O(rows × cols) time**, and the buckets hold every value once: **O(rows × cols) space**. Walking each diagonal directly has the same complexity — the bucket version just has far fewer places for an off-by-one bug to hide.
Edge cases to test

items: **One row** — every value is its own diagonal.
**Non-square** — `2 × 4` has 5 diagonals, the longest of length 2.

blocks.text: Where this idea shows up again

Diagonals running the **other** way (top-left to bottom-right) share a constant `r − c` instead. That can be negative, so add `cols − 1` to use it as an index. The N-Queens problem uses both keys to check diagonals in O(1). The general trick — **find the quantity that stays constant across the group you care about, and use it as a key** — is worth remembering far beyond grids.
